name: Rolling Kimura
summary: The Rolling Kimura is a dynamic Kimura Trap bottom technique where a figure-four grip on the opponent's arm powers a roll-through that simultaneously threatens the shoulder lock and sweeps you up into back control or top kimura trap.
description: Master the Rolling Kimura from Kimura Trap bottom in BJJ. Use the figure-four grip to roll through, threatening the shoulder lock while sweeping up to back control.
overview:
Rooted in the Kimura Trap bottom system, the Rolling Kimura turns a defensive-looking bottom position into a launching pad for sweeps and back takes. Once you own a deep figure-four on the opponent's arm, their attempts to posture, drive forward, or extract the limb supply the very momentum you need: you roll through the trapped shoulder, dragging them over the top while their arm stays loaded with submission pressure.

The rolling motion is what makes the technique punch above its weight. Rotational momentum multiplies the leverage on the shoulder far beyond what arm strength alone could generate, so size and strength matter far less than timing. The opponent is caught in a genuine dilemma: defend the kimura by keeping the elbow tight and they feed the sweep; fight the sweep by basing out and they expose the shoulder. When the roll completes you typically arrive in back control, in a top kimura trap, or, if the roll stalls, in a neutral turtle scramble rather than back on the bottom.

The technique works in both gi and no-gi, though the connection differs. In the gi, cloth grips on the sleeve or lapel supplement the figure-four and slow the opponent's escape; in no-gi the lock relies on tight wrist-and-elbow control and a closer body connection because the reduced friction lets a sweaty arm slip. Either way, the roll itself, not the squeeze, is the engine, which is why the Rolling Kimura remains a cornerstone of the modern half guard and Kimura Trap attacking system.
conditions: Secured figure-four kimura grip on one of the opponent's arms from a bottom position such as half guard or Kimura Trap bottom
Opponent is posting, posturing, or driving weight forward, loading the connection needed to power the roll
The trapped arm is controlled near the elbow rather than the wrist for maximum rotational control of the shoulder
Your hips remain mobile and are not fully flattened, allowing you to initiate the rotation
Sufficient mat space to complete a full roll without obstruction

variants_and_adaptations.description: Without cloth grips the figure-four is established through direct wrist and elbow control, and the roll demands a tighter body connection because reduced friction lets a sweaty arm slip free. Extra emphasis goes on pinning the trapped wrist to the opponent's back and keeping your chest glued to their shoulder throughout the rotation.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: No-gi training, MMA, or whenever the opponent's gi is too sweaty to trust a sleeve or lapel grip

variants_and_adaptations.description: As you initiate the roll, thread one leg across to trap the opponent's free arm, arriving in the crucifix with both arms controlled instead of finishing the sweep cleanly. This trades a touch of sweep speed for total upper-body control and a buffet of undefended back attacks.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the opponent defends the kimura strongly with their free arm, or when locking down both arms is worth more than a fast back take

variants_and_adaptations.description: When the opponent widens their base and posts a heavy far leg to stop the roll, abandon the full rotation and hook that exposed far ankle, converting the kimura grip into a classic Old School sweep up to the top instead.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the opponent successfully bases out against the roll but leaves the far leg available to hook

variants_and_adaptations.description: Rather than rolling toward the trapped-arm side, reverse the rotation and roll the opposite way over your other shoulder. This changes the angle of attack on the shoulder joint and catches opponents who have committed to defending the standard direction.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When the opponent anticipates and walls off the conventional rolling direction, or when wall and mat space force the other way

position_integration: The Rolling Kimura is a central branch of the Kimura Trap bottom system, sharing its figure-four grip with the Old School Sweep, the Kimura Sweep, and Kimura to Back Take. From half guard bottom the same grip that threatens the shoulder lock also off-balances the top player, so the Rolling Kimura is simply the reaction you choose when the opponent drives forward or rolls to relieve pressure rather than basing wide. Each defensive response opens a different branch: a wide base feeds the Old School sweep, a forward drive feeds the roll, and a turn into the grip feeds the back take. Understanding the Rolling Kimura as one spoke of this interconnected grip-based hub, rather than an isolated trick, is what lets you flow between sweeps, back takes, and submissions off a single point of control.

attacker.name: Rolling Kimura Attacker
attacker.description: How to execute the Rolling Kimura in BJJ. Attacking perspective with setup, execution steps, counters, and training progressions from Kimura Trap bottom.
attacker.overview: The Rolling Kimura from Kimura Trap bottom converts the figure-four grip into a dynamic sweep and back-take engine. Rather than waiting to finish a static shoulder lock, you use the opponent's posture and forward pressure against them: as they drive in or fight to free the arm, you roll through the trapped shoulder, dragging their upper body over the top while the kimura stays loaded. The dual threat is what makes it so hard to stop, because every honest answer to the submission helps the sweep and every honest answer to the sweep endangers the shoulder. A clean roll lands you in back control with hooks available, in a top kimura trap with the grip intact, or, at worst, in a neutral turtle scramble on top rather than stuck on the bottom. The rolling momentum multiplies your leverage, so the technique stays effective against bigger, stronger opponents when your timing and connection are right.
key_principles: Secure a deep figure-four near the opponent's elbow before committing to the roll, because a shallow wrist grip slips during rotation and surrenders the sweep
Let the opponent's forward pressure power the roll; you supply the timing and direction, not raw strength
Keep your hips and chest connected to the opponent throughout the rotation so you sweep them with you instead of rolling away underneath them
Maintain constant shoulder pressure through the grip so every defensive choice feeds either the sweep or the submission
Initiate the roll when the opponent drives in or postures, not when they are settled and based wide; read their weight before you commit
Have your finish chosen before you roll: back control, top kimura trap, or crucifix, based on what their free arm and base are doing
Consolidate the instant the roll completes, because the transition window is where the position is won or lost
setup_requirements: A secured figure-four kimura grip on one of the opponent's arms from half guard bottom, Kimura Trap bottom, or a scramble
Control of the trapped arm near the elbow so the rotation loads the shoulder rather than just the wrist
Mobile hips that are not flattened, allowing you to turn and initiate the rotation
An opponent who is posting, posturing, or driving forward so the connection has momentum to redirect
Enough mat space to complete a full roll without hitting an obstacle or the cage
A free hand or framing leg ready to control the opponent's far side or block their counter-roll

execution_steps.action: Secure and deepen the kimura grip
execution_steps.description: From half guard or Kimura Trap bottom, lock the figure-four on the opponent's arm: your near hand grips their wrist while your other hand threads under their arm and clamps your own wrist. Slide the grip up toward their elbow so the lock controls the shoulder joint, not just the hand, and pin their trapped wrist toward their own back to pre-load the rotation.

execution_steps.action: Read the weight and bait the drive
execution_steps.description: Keep your elbows tight and your hips live, threatening the shoulder lock just enough that the opponent reacts. The roll needs their weight moving toward you, so either wait for them to posture and drive forward to flatten you, or bump your hips to provoke that forward pressure. Initiating against a settled, wide base wastes the roll and stalls you in a stuck position.

execution_steps.action: Turn to your side and set the rolling angle
execution_steps.description: As they bring weight forward, turn onto the shoulder of your trapped-arm side and tuck that shoulder under, creating the diagonal axis you will roll across. Bring your knees toward your chest to compact your body so the rotation is tight and fast rather than long and slow, keeping the figure-four glued to your sternum the whole time.

execution_steps.action: Initiate the roll, pulling the shoulder under
execution_steps.description: Drive off your feet and roll diagonally over your tucked shoulder, pulling the kimura grip tight to your chest so the opponent's trapped shoulder leads the rotation. Their loaded arm forces their upper body to follow you over the top: they either roll or take shoulder damage. Stay compact and keep the grip locked so the loaded joint does the steering.

execution_steps.action: Stay connected and surface on top
execution_steps.description: Throughout the roll keep your chest and hips wrapped to the opponent so you come up on top of them, not beside them. Use your free hand to post and steer the rotation and to stop them sliding off your hips. The goal is to surface chest-to-back, having rolled them over rather than spinning yourself away into open space.

execution_steps.action: Read the landing and choose the finish
execution_steps.description: As you come up, assess what the opponent gave you. If their back is exposed, drive to back control and prepare your hooks. If their free arm is within reach of your legs, trap it for the crucifix. If the grip is still dominant with their arm behind their back, settle into top kimura trap and hunt the finish. The opening they leave dictates the choice you committed to before rolling.

Lock down your chosen finish without pausing. For back control, secure the seatbelt and both hooks with chest-to-back pressure. For crucifix, pin the free arm between your legs while keeping the kimura. For the top kimura, walk your hips toward their head and rotate the arm to finish. Speed here decides whether you keep the advantage or let them scramble out during the transition.

common_counters.counter: Opponent bases out wide with a heavy far leg and posts to refuse the roll
common_counters.your_response: Do not force the rotation into a strong base. Hook the exposed far ankle and convert to an Old School sweep, or switch your hips to chase the back take instead, since their wide base feeds those branches more readily than the roll.

common_counters.counter: Opponent counter-rolls with your momentum to come out on top
common_counters.your_response: Never release the figure-four. Ride their counter-roll and finish the kimura from wherever you land, or if they overshoot, extend the arm into an armbar as they pass neutral. The grip keeps you in the fight even when the roll goes their way.

common_counters.counter: Opponent strips or straightens the trapped arm before you commit
common_counters.your_response: Re-pin the wrist to their back and re-establish the figure-four at the elbow before rolling. If the grip is truly gone, switch to the opposite arm or chain to another half guard sweep rather than rolling into nothing.

common_counters.counter: Opponent drops the trapped shoulder and follows the rotation early
common_counters.your_response: This helps you. Follow their shoulder through the roll and keep rotating, because their compliance usually exposes the back even faster, so drive straight to the hooks and seatbelt for back control.

common_counters.counter: Opponent frames their free forearm into your hip to block the rotation
common_counters.your_response: Collapse the frame with your chest and free hand before initiating, or trap that framing arm with your leg and roll into the crucifix, taking both arms with you and converting their defense into your most controlling finish.

common_errors.error: Rolling away from the opponent instead of rolling them over you
common_errors.consequence: You spin out from under them and surface on the bottom or give up the grip, often ending in their guard or worse
common_errors.correction: Keep your hips and chest wrapped to the opponent the whole roll; think of rolling around and over them, never away from them

common_errors.error: Loosening the figure-four during the rotation
common_errors.consequence: The opponent frees the arm, kills the submission threat, and rides out the roll to land on top
common_errors.correction: The grip should tighten as you roll; the loaded shoulder is what drags them over, so glue the figure-four to your chest

common_errors.error: Initiating the roll against a settled, wide base
common_errors.consequence: There is no momentum to redirect, the opponent simply posts, and you burn energy spinning into a stuck position
common_errors.correction: Bait or wait for the forward drive and roll on their weight coming in, not when they are heavy and based out

common_errors.error: Rolling straight backward instead of diagonally over the tucked shoulder
common_errors.consequence: Flat mechanics produce weak, slow leverage and give the opponent time to strip the grip or base out
common_errors.correction: Tuck the trapped-side shoulder and roll diagonally across it at roughly 45 degrees to load the joint progressively through the arc

common_errors.error: Having no finish chosen before the roll
common_errors.consequence: You complete the rotation but hesitate, and the opponent escapes during the transition window
common_errors.correction: Decide back control, crucifix, or top kimura before you commit, and read their free arm and base on the way up

common_errors.error: Powering the roll with arm strength instead of body momentum
common_errors.consequence: The technique gasses you out and stalls against bigger opponents who can resist an arm-only pull
common_errors.correction: Drive the rotation with your legs, hips, and the opponent's own forward pressure; the arms only maintain the grip

training_progressions.focus: Securing the figure-four and setting the rolling angle from Kimura Trap bottom
training_progressions.description: Practice locking the figure-four from half guard and Kimura Trap bottom with a stationary partner. Focus on correct hand placement, grip depth at the elbow, pinning the trapped wrist, and turning onto the trapped-side shoulder to set the diagonal axis. Partner provides zero resistance. Aim for 30 repetitions per session.

training_progressions.focus: Developing a smooth roll while keeping the grip and connection
training_progressions.description: Execute the full roll with a passive partner. Focus on keeping hips and chest wrapped to the opponent, maintaining grip tension, and surfacing on top rather than spinning away. Drill both rolling directions for 20 to 30 repetitions per session to build the muscle memory for the diagonal shoulder roll.

training_progressions.focus: Timing the roll to the opponent's weight and defensive choices
training_progressions.description: Partner cycles through light reactions: driving forward, basing wide, fighting the grip, and framing the hip. Practice baiting the forward drive, timing the roll to incoming weight, and branching to Old School or the back take when the roll is walled off. Develop the feel for when the opponent is most vulnerable to the rotation.

training_progressions.focus: Executing against moderate to strong resistance
training_progressions.description: Partner uses grip fighting, base management, counter-rolls, and attempts to flatten you. Practice timing the roll for vulnerable moments and transitioning in real time between the Rolling Kimura, Old School sweep, crucifix, and back take based on their reactions. Begin recognizing which finish is available as you surface.

training_progressions.focus: Applying the technique in live sparring from Kimura Trap bottom
training_progressions.description: Start in Kimura Trap bottom in 3 to 5 minute positional rounds against full defense. Work setups, feints, and grip fights that create the forward pressure you need, and chain the Rolling Kimura with the rest of the Kimura Trap system to build a complete bottom attacking game.

training_progressions.focus: Building a complete Kimura Trap bottom system around the roll
training_progressions.description: Integrate the Rolling Kimura into your half guard and Kimura Trap game as one branch of a connected attack web. Develop the ability to read defensive patterns and pick the highest-percentage option, and study high-level gi and no-gi footage of the grip-based bottom system.

flashcards.question: When is the optimal moment to initiate the Rolling Kimura from Kimura Trap bottom?
flashcards.answer: Roll when the opponent brings their weight toward you, as they posture up and drive forward to flatten you, or as they fight to extract the trapped arm. That incoming pressure is the momentum you redirect. Initiating against a settled, wide base gives you nothing to roll on, so bait the drive or wait for it rather than forcing the rotation into a heavy, balanced opponent.

flashcards.question: What grip detail most determines whether the roll succeeds, and where should it sit?
flashcards.answer: The figure-four must sit deep at the opponent's elbow, not their wrist, with their trapped wrist pinned toward their own back. A shallow wrist grip lets the arm straighten and slip during rotation, killing both the sweep and the submission. The elbow-deep lock controls the shoulder joint itself, so the loaded shoulder leads the roll and drags the opponent's upper body over the top with you.

flashcards.question: Which direction do you roll, and why does the diagonal angle matter?
flashcards.answer: Tuck your trapped-side shoulder and roll diagonally across it at roughly a 45-degree angle rather than straight backward. The diagonal axis loads the shoulder joint progressively through the arc and keeps your body wrapped tight to the opponent, preserving the chest and hip connection that sweeps them over you. A flat backward roll produces weak, slow leverage and hands the opponent time to strip the grip or base out.

flashcards.question: What is the single most common reason a Rolling Kimura dumps the attacker onto the bottom?
flashcards.answer: Rolling away from the opponent instead of rolling them over you. If your hips and chest separate from their body during the rotation, you spin out underneath them and surface on the bottom, often in their guard. Keep your chest and hips wrapped around the opponent the entire time so you roll around and over them, taking them with you rather than vacating the space they fall into.

flashcards.question: Your opponent widens their base and posts a heavy far leg to refuse the roll. What do you do?
flashcards.answer: Do not fight a strong base with the rotation. Their wide base exposes the far ankle, so hook it and convert the kimura grip into an Old School sweep up to the top, or shift your hips to chase the back take instead. The Rolling Kimura is one branch of the Kimura Trap system, so when the roll is walled off, the same grip feeds the sweep and back-take branches: flow to whichever the opponent's reaction opens.

flashcards.question: The opponent counter-rolls with your momentum and threatens to come up on top. How do you respond?
flashcards.answer: Never let go of the figure-four. Ride their counter-roll and finish the kimura from wherever you land, since you frequently surface in a top kimura trap anyway. If they overcommit and roll past neutral, release the figure-four and extend the arm into an armbar as they pass. The grip keeps you dangerous regardless of which way the roll resolves, so the cardinal rule is to keep it locked.

flashcards.question: What must be true about your hips before you can launch the roll?
flashcards.answer: Your hips must be live and off the mat, not flattened. The Rolling Kimura needs you to turn onto your trapped-side shoulder and compact your knees toward your chest to set the diagonal axis, which is impossible if the opponent has pancaked your hips to the floor. If you are being flattened, first re-insert a knee shield or recover hip mobility, because the roll is launched from an active, turned hip, not a flat back.

flashcards.question: You complete the roll and come up on top. How do you decide between back control, crucifix, and the top kimura?
flashcards.answer: Read what the opponent gave you on the way up. An exposed back with their arm out of the picture means drive to back control and insert hooks for the highest-value finish. A reachable free arm means trap it between your legs for the crucifix and both-arm control. A still-dominant grip with their arm pinned behind their back means settle into top kimura trap and finish the shoulder. The opening dictates the choice, so decide before you roll and confirm on the way up.

flashcards.question: Why must the figure-four tighten rather than loosen during the rotation?
flashcards.answer: The roll works because the loaded shoulder forces the opponent to rotate with you or accept joint damage, and that pressure is the steering wheel. If the grip loosens mid-roll, the threat evaporates, the opponent frees the arm, and they ride out the rotation to land on top. Pull the figure-four tight to your sternum so it actually tightens as you roll, because the squeeze and the sweep are the same action.

flashcards.question: The opponent jams their free forearm into your hip to block the rotation. What are your options?
flashcards.answer: Either collapse the frame before you commit by driving your chest and free hand into it to flatten the arm, or use the frame against them by trapping that framing arm with your leg and rolling into the crucifix. Taking the free arm with you on the roll converts their defensive frame into a both-arms-trapped finish, so a stubborn frame becomes the entry to your most controlling outcome.

attacker.safety_considerations: The Rolling Kimura loads the shoulder joint under rotational momentum, so it must be drilled with strict progression: start with zero resistance and add speed only over weeks. The attacker must keep the rotation controlled and never jerk or spike the roll, since the combination of body momentum and a locked figure-four can injure the shoulder even without a deliberate finish. Communicate clearly with your partner, drill on soft mats while learning the roll, and have both players confirm tap protocols beforehand. Defenders should tap early to shoulder pressure rather than riding it out, because torn shoulder ligaments and labrum injuries carry long recoveries. In hard rolling and competition, respect that the dynamic nature of the roll can create unexpected joint loading mid-rotation, so maintain awareness and protect your partner at all times.

defender.name: Rolling Kimura Defender
defender.description: How to defend against the Rolling Kimura in BJJ. Recognition cues, grip defense, and counters for the top player facing a Kimura Trap bottom roll.
defender.overview: Defending the Rolling Kimura means stopping a bottom player who has already secured a figure-four on your arm from converting it into a sweep or back take. You face the same dilemma you are trying to impose on others: protect the trapped shoulder from the kimura while refusing to be rolled over the top. The decisive truth is that prevention beats cure, because once the bottom player has a deep elbow grip and your weight commits forward, the roll becomes very hard to stop. Your highest-percentage defense is winning the grip fight before the figure-four locks and keeping the trapped elbow tight to your own body. If the grip is already set, your job shifts to denying the roll: keep a wide, heavy base, avoid driving your weight blindly forward into the rotation, and be ready to ride or counter-roll so that if you are taken over, you land on top with the attacker dumped onto the bottom rather than surrendering your back.
key_principles: Win the grip fight early and strip the figure-four before it locks deep at your elbow, because a wrist-level grip is far easier to clear
Keep the threatened elbow pinned tight to your own ribs so the arm cannot be isolated or loaded
Maintain a wide, heavy base and avoid committing your weight blindly forward, since your forward drive is the fuel the roll needs
If the grip is locked, post the far hand and far leg to wall off the rotation before it starts
Protect the shoulder first and the position second; tap to genuine joint pressure rather than risking the arm to save the back
If you are being rolled, ride it and counter-roll to land on top rather than fighting to stay put and feeding the back take
Stay aware of the secondary branches, because basing wide invites the Old School sweep and turning in invites the back take
recognition_cues: The bottom player threads one arm under yours and clamps a figure-four on your wrist, sliding the grip up toward your elbow
Your trapped wrist is dragged toward your own back, loading the shoulder and pre-setting the rotation
The bottom player turns onto the shoulder of your trapped-arm side and compacts their knees toward their chest
You feel rotational pressure building on your shoulder the instant you post or drive your weight forward
Their hips dig under yours and their chest wraps tight to you, the signature connection that precedes the roll

defensive_options.action: Strip the figure-four with your free hand and retract the trapped elbow tight to your ribs
defensive_options.when_to_use: The instant you feel the grip being threaded under your arm or clamped on your wrist, before it locks deep at the elbow
defensive_options.if_successful: The grip dies, the back take is off the table, and you keep top control to continue passing
defensive_options.risk: Diving both hands to the grip can lighten your base and open a sweep or a different attack if you are slow

defensive_options.action: Widen your base and post your far hand and far leg to wall off the rotation
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the figure-four is already locked but the roll has not started; keep your weight off the trapped side
defensive_options.if_successful: Without an axis to roll across, the attacker cannot sweep you up to the top kimura and the attack stalls
defensive_options.risk: A wide base exposes the far ankle to an Old School sweep, so be ready to defend that branch

defensive_options.action: Ride the roll and counter-roll, driving your weight through their rotation to land on top
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the roll is already underway and you cannot stop it; commit to coming out on top rather than resisting in place
defensive_options.if_successful: You surface on top with the attacker dumped onto the bottom in turtle, and the kimura grip is weakened by the angle change
defensive_options.risk: Mistimed, the counter-roll accelerates their sweep and feeds you straight to back control

defensive_options.action: Pin the shoulder safe and straighten the trapped arm to clear it as the roll loads
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the grip is set but shallow toward your wrist, giving you room to extend and slip the arm free
defensive_options.if_successful: The arm slips the figure-four, the rotational threat dissolves, and the exchange resets to a neutral scramble
defensive_options.risk: Straightening into a deep elbow grip can hand the attacker an even tighter kimura or an armbar

favorable_outcomes.how: When you cannot prevent the roll, ride it instead of fighting it in place: post your free hand, follow the attacker's rotation, and drive your weight through so that as the roll completes you surface on top and the attacker lands on the bottom in turtle. Time the counter-roll to the peak of their momentum, keep the shoulder safe, and immediately pressure them down before they re-establish the grip.

common_errors.error: Letting the figure-four lock deep before you start fighting the grip
common_errors.consequence: Once the elbow-deep grip is set and your weight commits forward, the roll becomes extremely hard to stop
common_errors.correction: React to the first contact on your wrist by peeling the grip and tucking the elbow to your ribs before it slides to the elbow

common_errors.error: Driving your weight blindly forward into the bottom player
common_errors.consequence: Your forward pressure is exactly the momentum the roll feeds on, so you power your own sweep
common_errors.correction: Keep a wide, heavy, controlled base and post off to the side; do not lunge your weight over a player who has your arm

common_errors.error: Fighting to stay put once the roll has clearly started
common_errors.consequence: Resisting in place lets the loaded shoulder drag you over slowly and surrenders your back
common_errors.correction: When the roll is unavoidable, commit to riding and counter-rolling so you land on top instead of being taken over

common_errors.error: Ignoring the shoulder to save the position
common_errors.consequence: Riding out heavy rotational pressure risks a torn shoulder for the sake of a position you may lose anyway
common_errors.correction: Protect the joint first and tap to genuine kimura pressure rather than gambling your shoulder on a scramble

common_errors.error: Basing wide without respecting the secondary sweeps
common_errors.consequence: A wide base stops the roll but feeds the Old School sweep off your exposed far leg
common_errors.correction: Pair the wide base with active far-leg awareness, keeping the ankle out of reach or staying ready to defend the hook

flashcards.question: What is the highest-percentage window to defend the Rolling Kimura?
flashcards.answer: Before the figure-four locks deep. The moment you feel the bottom player thread under your arm and clamp your wrist, you have a brief window to strip the grip and tuck your elbow tight to your ribs. Once the grip slides to your elbow and your weight commits forward, the loaded shoulder lets them roll you at will, and your defensive success rate drops sharply, so win the grip fight early rather than trying to out-muscle a locked roll.

flashcards.question: Your opponent has locked the kimura grip from the bottom but has not rolled yet. What is your best defense?
flashcards.answer: Widen your base and post your far hand and far leg to deny the rotational axis, while keeping your weight off the trapped-arm side so you do not feed the roll. Keep the threatened elbow tight and avoid driving forward. Without a diagonal axis to roll across, the attacker cannot generate the sweep, but stay alert to the far ankle, because a wide base invites the Old School sweep as the next branch.

flashcards.question: Why is driving your weight forward into a Kimura Trap bottom player so dangerous?
flashcards.answer: Your forward pressure is the engine of the Rolling Kimura. The bottom player times the roll to your incoming weight, redirecting it so you roll over the top while your shoulder stays loaded. Lunging forward into a player who already controls your arm essentially powers your own sweep and back take. Keep a wide, controlled base and post to the side instead of committing your weight over them.

flashcards.question: The roll has already started and you cannot stop it. What do you do?
flashcards.answer: Stop fighting to stay put and commit to riding the roll. Post your free hand, follow their rotation, and drive your weight through so you land on top with the attacker dumped onto the bottom in turtle. Counter-rolling at the peak of their momentum weakens the grip's angle and is far better than being slowly dragged over into a surrendered back. Throughout, keep the shoulder safe and tap to real joint pressure.

flashcards.question: Why should shoulder safety take priority over keeping the position when defending the Rolling Kimura?
flashcards.answer: Because the technique loads the shoulder under rotational momentum, riding out heavy kimura pressure to save a position risks a torn labrum or ligaments with a long recovery. A lost position is recoverable in seconds, but a blown-out shoulder costs months. If you feel genuine joint pressure and your counter is not there, tap, because protecting the arm keeps you training, which matters more than any single exchange.

training_progressions.focus: Spotting the figure-four early and stripping it before it locks
training_progressions.description: Partner slowly threads and clamps the kimura grip from the bottom while you drill recognizing the first contact and peeling the grip with your free hand, tucking the elbow to your ribs. Use zero resistance at first, building to light resistance as your reaction speed improves.

training_progressions.focus: Denying the roll once the grip is locked
training_progressions.description: Partner locks the grip and tries to set the rolling axis with moderate effort. Drill widening your base, posting the far hand and leg, keeping weight off the trapped side, and refusing to drive forward. Build the automatic habit of basing rather than lunging when your arm is controlled.

training_progressions.focus: Riding the roll to land on top
training_progressions.description: Partner initiates the full roll while you drill riding it and counter-rolling to surface on top with them on the bottom. Start at half speed to develop timing, then build to full speed. Emphasize posting the free hand, protecting the shoulder, and pressuring them down immediately on landing.

training_progressions.focus: Defending the Rolling Kimura under full resistance
training_progressions.description: Start in Kimura Trap top with the bottom player working the full system, including the Rolling Kimura, Old School sweep, and back take. Drill distinguishing the roll from the other branches and responding with the right defense in real time, integrating shoulder safety and base management under live pressure.
